This includes ensuring its seamless articulation with the United Nations governance architecture and establishing a predictable, sustainable funding model rooted in voluntary contributions. Be sure that Portugal remains fully engaged in these collective efforts to ensure that scientific knowledge serves the common good and drives transformative policy action worldwide. I thank you.
Thank you very much, Your Excellency, Mr. Xavier. We now move to Venezuela.

Mr. President, the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela welcomes the convening of this meeting, which is essential to tackling one of the most urgent and historical debts of the global order. Inequality is not just an imbalance in the distribution of income. It is a structural challenge which is decisive and that fundamentally affects access to education, health, food, decent work and development financing. At the end of the day, this gap, this perpetual gap, limits the fundamental right of peoples to build a future with justice and dignity. It's therefore insufficient to confine ourselves to diagnosing the consequences of inequality. We must act on the structural causes and the systemic mechanisms that reproduce it, both internally and on the international stage. At the national level, the fundamental priority must be the human being. That means consolidating robust social protection, strengthening essential public services, encouraging sovereign production, and generating effective opportunities real opportunities so that economic development can be reflected directly in social welfare. However, sovereign efforts of our nations require, of course, a global environment that is favorable and that does not limit the possibilities for progress. Mr. President, today there are profound and unacceptable imbalances in the global economic structure which restrict equitable access to markets, technology and financing. Overcoming those imbalances demands a true refounding of the international financial architecture in the interest of a truly inclusive, representative and solidarity-based model that can meet the diversity and real needs of the global South. Venezuela therefore advocates for the establishment of this panel on inequality, contributing with scientific rigor and production of evidence to identifying real solutions that can be reflected in better public policies and better international cooperation. We therefore reaffirm that it's essential and indispensable and urgent that we eradicate all of the measures that smother the development of the nations. Unilateral coercive measures, known as sanctions, are a flagrant violation of international law and a deliberate obstacle that restricts the financial and productive capacities of states, worsening vulnerability and inequality for millions of people, Mr. President. Reducing inequality is not only a technical goal to close statistical gaps. It's an ethical and political imperative for guaranteeing social cohesion, peace, and the sovereignty of our nations. This cause demands sovereign responsibility, but also international cooperation strengthened in solidarity and mutual respect. The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela reiterates its staunch commitment to contributing decisively to this collective task. Thank you very much.
Thank you very much, Your Excellency Pimentel, for your input. We now go to Bangladesh.

Excellencies, colleagues, We thank the governments of Brazil, Norway, Spain and South Africa for organizing this event. We welcome the proposed International Panel on Inequality. Global inequality remains a serious concern. The richest 10% receive 52% of global income and own about 76% of global wealth. In contrast, the poorest half receives only 8.5% of income and own just mere 2% of wealth. And nearly 700 million people live in extreme poverty today. There are new factors that are widening existing inequality and creating new inequalities. Climate change is increasing the inequalities. Around 1.2 billion people face serious climate risk. The most vulnerable suffer the most, who do not contribute to the crisis at all. Digital inequality is another concern. One third of the world's population are not connected online. In high-income countries, internet use reached 93%, but only 27% in low-income countries. The COVID-19 pandemic also exposed deep inequalities in healthcare. By May 2022, about 80% of people in high-income countries had received at least one vaccine dose, compared to only 60% in low-income countries. These existing inequalities erode trust, weaken social bond, and hinder progress towards SDGs. Bangladesh is determined to bridge this gap by restoring rights, building accountable institutions, protecting human dignity, and ensuring fair and inclusive development. Our experience shows that reducing inequality requires sustained action and investment. In this spirit, we wish to offer four proposals. First, To reinforce global cooperation to expand access to education, jobs, skills, and equal opportunities for youth and women, especially in developing countries. Second, to strengthen global support for climate-vulnerable countries to prevent climate displacement and protect affected people. Third, to promote global cooperation for affordable internet, digital skills, and fair access to AI so that no one is left behind. And finally, to create a global health equity mechanism to ensure timely access to vaccines, therapeutics, diagnostics, and essential health technologies in developing countries during future pandemics. To conclude, we expect the panel to turn evidence into practical action to reduce inequality and expand opportunities. We hope its work will provide greater support to most vulnerable people across the countries. I thank you.

Thank you very much. We now conclude the section of UN member states. And now we go to intergovernmental organizations and UN entities. And the time allocated is two minutes per each. I will now start with the UN-Habitat.

Excellencies, inequality is most visible in cities. The global housing crisis exposes a severe affordability challenge at planetary scale. Young people not able to buy or rent a house, elderly, persons with disability not able to access or sometimes stay in their homes. It exposes 300 million people living in homelessness situation, plus 1 billion people living in informal settlement. Yet, access to housing is fundamental to achieve the sustainable development goals. Yet, building housing right is critical for us to address the climate change. Housing crisis in cities are the face of inequalities globally. Thank you.
Thank you very much, UN-Habitat. We now go to the International Labour Organization.

The proposed international panel on inequality and the co-host for bringing this important discussion to you and sustaining political momentum on one of the defining challenges of our time. Rising inequalities, both within and between countries, jeopardize the achievement of the sustainable development goals and weaken social cohesion and trust in institution and constrain sustainable economic prosperity. Addressing inequality is therefore central to social justice and sustainable development. Since its foundation, the ILO has been guided by the conviction that the world of work is a critical arena for understanding and addressing inequalities. A key lesson from the ILO's experience is that reducing inequality requires actions on both pre-distribution and redistribution. Decent work, adequate wages, skills, and strong labor market institutions are essential to tackle inequality at its source. This also means addressing market concentration and market power, which can affect workers' income and widen inequality, both between firms and workers, and also among the firms, especially between large firms and SMEs. Effective, inclusive social protection is equally essential It should not simply mop up, default out of the economic policies, but form part of the social infrastructure that works along with economic and labor market policies. The effort to reduce inequality must also address the structural barriers faced by women, migrant workers, persons with disabilities, indigenous people and ethnic minorities. The ILO remains ready to contribute its expertise on labour market inequalities, wages, market power, gender equality and social protection, informality and social dialogue, and we very much look forward to engaging constructively with the member states partners as this initiative evolved. Thank you very much.
Thank you. We will now go to Iceland.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it's a pleasure to join you here today to discuss the challenge of inequality and how we can collectively take steps to address it. Persistent inequalities in income, wealth, and opportunities undermine trust in institutions and deny too many people the opportunity to fulfill their potential. Inequality is not inevitable, and it's in our shared interest to better understand its causes and find effective ways to address it. Government of Iceland's stated aim is to prioritize the public interest and public welfare above particular or private interests. However, countering things like extreme market concentration and unequal wealth distribution domestically is not sufficient. Persistent inequalities can undermine trust, not only within societies, but also in the multilateral order itself. We see this initiative as an important contribution to strengthening multilateral cooperation. Iceland strongly believes in science-based and evidence-informed policymaking. We therefore welcome the proposal to establish an International Panel on Inequality. An independent international panel anchored in neutral, objective and science-based analysis could serve as a global resource for policymakers, the private sector, civil society and the public. Iceland is pleased to support the vision statement and to join those countries supporting this initiative. We thank the governments of South Africa, Brazil, Spain and Norway for this initiative and we look forward to continuing this important discussion. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Iceland. We now go to the United Nations Research Institute for Social Development.

The United Nations Research Institute for Social Development, UNRIS, is delighted to see the growing momentum behind the proposed International Panel on Inequality. As the UN Research Institute dedicated for over 60 years to advancing research on the often neglected challenges of social development, we strongly welcome this initiative. For decades, UNRIS research has shown that inequality is not only an economic issue. It affects opportunity, voice, social cohesion, trust in institutions, and the prospect of sustainable development. We therefore welcome the vision of an independent, science-based body that can bring together and assess the best available knowledge on inequality from around the world. We are convinced that the proposed panel can strengthen the foundations for informed and effective action to address inequality within and between countries. ANRIS has been honored to support this process from its early stage and to host the inaugural meeting of the founding committee in Geneva in March 2026. That gathering demonstrates the growing commitment of governments, researchers, and international organizations to advancing a shared understanding of inequality and the actions needed to address it. We express our full support for the establishment of the IPI and encourage member states to support this effort politically and financially. Investing in evidence, knowledge, and multilateral cooperation is essential if we are to build more equitable, inclusive, and sustainable societies for all. Thank you.
Thank you very much. We now go to the United Nations University.

Excellencies, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the United Nations University, UNU, and its Rector, Professor Chulizi Marwala. Thank you to the governments of South Africa, Brazil, Norway and Spain, as well as the Deputy Secretary-General, for convening this important discussion. UNU serves as the academic arm and global think tank of the UN and is uniquely positioned within the UN system as an autonomous organ of the General Assembly that has full academic freedom. UNU conducts research to advance the understanding of the trends and drivers of inequalities, both globally and within countries. It analyses which policies and public actions are more and less successful at creating greater equality and questions how and why efforts to reduce inequality have not always been sufficient to reduce enduring inequalities. UNU very much welcomes the IPI initiative and is deeply honoured to be considered as its host. Effective policy making requires trusted evidence. It also requires the ability to bring together knowledge from different disciplines, regions and perspectives, especially from the global south. Across UNU research, we see how inequality intersects with development, education, technology, climate change, migration, governance, peace building and so on. These challenges are deeply interconnected and require integrated, evidence-based solutions. UNU stands ready to support efforts that strengthen the link between independent research and policy action. As an autonomous institution within the UN system with a mandate for academic freedom, we believe that credible evidence is one of the most important tools available to address these complex global challenges. We therefore welcome the momentum behind the panel and look forward to working with Member States and partners to advance this important initiative. I thank you.
Thank you very much. We now call upon the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.

OCHR welcomes this initiative. Inequality is not just an economic issue. It is fundamentally a human rights issue. It denies people equal opportunities, limits their voice and participation, and undermines the enjoyment of all human rights. Inequality is not only about income and wealth. It is also about power, who has a voice, who influences decisions, whose interests are represented and whether economic system work for everyone rather than a privileged few. Human rights therefore should be central to the work of the International Panel on Inequality. The panel can strengthen the evidence on the scale, drivers and consequences of inequality and assess which policy responses work. But evidence alone is not enough, human rights provide the framework for action They help clarify what must be done, who is accountable, and whether economic policies uphold the dignity and rights of all. The panel's work should drive change at the country level, helping governments expand fiscal space, strengthen public services, and social protection. Excellencies, the panel comes at a crucial moment as we accelerate progress towards 2030 and beyond. Current economic models are not delivering on reducing inequality. By placing human rights at the center, the panel can help build an economy, a human rights economy, that promotes equitable growth within and among countries, expands people's agency, and delivers dignity and sustainable prosperity for all. OSCHR looks forward to contributing to this effort. Thank you.

Thank you very much. That marks the end of our speakers list. I would now like to give the floor to Ms. Winnie Byanyima, the UN Under-Secretary-General and UNAIDS Executive Director and IPI founding committee member to briefly summarize the principal messages and commitment from this meeting. The detailed outcomes of the meeting will be reflected in the chair summary document that will be circulated to participants after the event. Following the presentation of the brief summary of the meeting outcomes by Ms. Banyima, I will briefly outline the next steps on the IPI establishment process before closing the meeting. Ms. Banyima, you will now have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. Excellencies, distinguished participants, ladies and gentlemen, Gentlemen, I'm honored to provide this summary. I will leave this meeting with a strong sense of hope because we have heard consistently from this discussion that inequality is not inevitable. It is a result of choices that are made. We heard, and these were not my words, that it is manmade. But because this is man-made, it can be unmade. We heard about wealth and income inequality at the national level, but also heard strong emphasis on the constraining role of international rules, including through global economic governance, on issues such as debt and tax. These undermine countries' ability to tackle inequality. We heard about the role that historical inequalities of colonialism have played. We were very pleased to hear clearly that the IPI is core to the achievement or the fulfillment of the promise of the UN Charter. and to the achievement of the 2030 agenda to leave no one behind. We heard consistently that the IPI is urgently needed by member states, civil society, the private sector, the entire international community. The key word here is science. There's a need for better scientific data, evidence analysis well organized so that it can be used at every level. We heard such strong welcome of the role that experts and academics on inequality can play on this issue and the important support that this can provide to policymakers. As we will hear more from Minister Lamola, we heard support in this room for the proposal of a UN General Assembly resolution for the establishment of the IPI. We heard about a strong operational model that is situated within the multilateral system and based on voluntary contributions. I'm pleased that we heard strong support not only from the champion founding member states of Brazil, Norway, South Africa, and Spain, but we heard from all regions, from Bangladesh, Barbados, Cape Verde, Iceland, Germany, Japan, Mexico, Portugal, and Venezuela, as well as from international organizations. This meeting provides a strong momentum to support and secure the establishment of the International Panel on Inequality. And I end by noting that the IPI is about people, because inequalities undermine human dignity, take away the right to health, the right to education, the right to social progress. It is not inevitable, and that is why we are here and that is why we are moving forward. Thank you, Chair.

I thank Ms. Bayima for her summary of the outcomes of the meeting. As indicated, a detailed chair summary will be circulated to all participants following the conclusion of this meeting. I would now like to outline the next steps towards the establishment of the IPI. Firstly, that there is a growing group of Member States and international organizations shaping the proposal for an International Panel on Inequality and building support for its establishment.

It is now key to form a mechanism in which Member States can formally guide and shape this future. All Member States will be invited to join in this effort.

Secondly.

There is momentum on the journey towards establishment at the United Nations, including working with multilateral agencies across the board, in particular with the UNDESA, and requesting to initially host the IPI at the UN University, in respect of its academic independence and autonomy.

Thirdly, and most notable, there is concrete commitment to securing a resolution at the UN General Assembly towards establishing the IPI, which the mechanisms will guide how we are going to go forward in doing such.

We look forward to your continued engagement and support through this next phase. Excellencies and ladies and gentlemen, as we come to an end of this meeting, I would like to thank you all for your attendance and participation.

I would also like to thank the UN Secretariat for their unwavering support in organizing this meeting.

They have been instrumental in this meeting's success.

Above all, I would like to thank all UN Member States, international organizations and civil society participants for their constructive participation. The insights and reflections heard here today are invaluable and will be instrumental in ensuring the successful establishment of the International Panel on Inequality.

Thank you all. The meeting is now adjourned. Thank you very much.

Thank you.
